title: Careers and Studies
description: Ten short stories about work and study: a job interview at a museum, a language exchange, a small coffee business, an attorney who becomes a painter, a new nurse, a summer at a newspaper, a lifeguard's first job, a science fair, choosing a college and a first book.

lessons.title: The Museum Job
lessons.summary: Nora prepares for a job interview at the city museum and gets the job.
lessons.text:
Nora had been looking for a job for 3 months. She had studied history in college, and she loved old things. One day, she saw that the city museum needed an assistant. The assistant would help visitors, answer the phone and work with the museum's team. "This is the job I want," Nora thought.

She sent her application, and a week later the museum called her. They wanted to meet her on Thursday at 3 in the afternoon.

Nora was excited, but she was also slightly afraid. She had never had a real job interview before. Her brother Ben helped her get ready. He asked her questions, and she answered them. Then she repeated her answers again and again until she felt comfortable. "Don't just repeat the same words like a machine," Ben reminded her. "Talk about what you love."

On Thursday, Nora put on a white shirt and dark pants. Ben looked at the shirt and smiled. "You look great," he said. He reminded her to leave early, because the buses were often late.

The interview was in a small office behind the main hall of the museum. A woman named Ms. Grant asked the questions. "This museum is very busy," she said. "On weekends, more than 2,000 people visit us. Are you aware of that?"

"Yes, I'm aware of it," Nora said. "I have visited the museum on many busy weekends. I enjoy being around people."

Then Ms. Grant asked, "If a child got lost in the museum, what would you do?" Nora thought for a moment. "I would stay calm. I would ask the child's name, and I would call the front desk." Ms. Grant smiled slightly and wrote something down.

The afternoon felt very long. Nora went home and waited by the phone. At 6 in the evening, the phone rang. It was Ms. Grant. "We would like you to be our new assistant," she said. "We are lucky to have you."

Nora told Ben the news. "I was so lucky," she said. "It wasn't luck," Ben said. "You were ready."

Questions:
What job did Nora want?
She wanted to be an assistant at the city museum.
When was the interview?
The interview was on Thursday at 3 in the afternoon.
How did Ben help Nora?
He asked her questions, and she repeated her answers until she felt comfortable.
What did Nora wear?
She wore a white shirt and dark pants.
What would Nora do if a child got lost?
She would stay calm, ask the child's name and call the front desk.
Why did Ben say it wasn't luck?
He said it wasn't luck because Nora was ready.

lessons.title: The Language Exchange
lessons.summary: Leo learns Polish with a language exchange partner and sings at a festival in Poland.
lessons.text:
Leo is 24 and works in an office in Chicago. His girlfriend, Anna, comes from a family from eastern Poland. This summer, Anna's family is having a big party in their small town in eastern Poland, and Leo is invited. There is one problem. Leo doesn't speak Polish, and Anna's grandparents speak neither English nor German.

So Leo has decided to learn Polish. He has been using an app for 2 months, but the app doesn't help him speak. So he joins a language exchange. Every Tuesday evening, he meets Piotr, a student from eastern Poland who is studying in Chicago. For half an hour, they speak English. Then, for half an hour, they speak Polish.

At first, speaking Polish scares Leo. The words are long, and the rules seem impossible. "Don't be scared," Piotr says. "Mistakes are normal. I make mistakes in English all the time." Leo is never mad at Piotr when Piotr corrects him. "If I got mad every time someone corrected me, I would never learn anything," Piotr says.

One evening, Piotr brings an old Polish children's story. It is about a young prince who leaves his castle to see the world. The sentences are short, so Leo can understand most of them. He reads the story about the prince 3 times.

Piotr also teaches Leo to sing an old Polish song. At first, Leo knows neither the words nor the music. But he practices every day, and soon he can sing it. "In my town, everyone sings this song at the summer festival," Piotr says.

In July, Leo and his girlfriend fly to Poland. The family party is during the town's summer festival. There is music, food and dancing in the main square. Anna's grandfather takes her hand and spins her around and around. Then he spins Leo, too, and everyone laughs.

When the band plays Piotr's song, Leo sings with everyone. Anna's grandparents are surprised and very happy. Now Leo can talk to them a little.

Questions:
Why does Leo want to learn Polish?
His girlfriend's family is from eastern Poland, and her grandparents speak neither English nor German.
Who is Piotr?
Piotr is a student from eastern Poland who is studying in Chicago.
How does Leo feel about speaking Polish at first?
At first, speaking Polish scares him.
What does Piotr say about getting mad?
He says that if he got mad every time someone corrected him, he would never learn anything.
What is the old story about?
It is about a young prince who leaves his castle to see the world.
What does Leo do at the festival?
When the band plays Piotr's song, he sings with everyone.

lessons.title: Cold Coffee in Bottles
lessons.summary: Carlos starts a small business selling cold coffee in bottles, and a chain of stores sells it.
lessons.text:
Carlos had worked in a coffee shop for 6 years. He knew everything about coffee, and he dreamed of having his own small business. One summer, he had an idea: he would make cold coffee and sell it in glass bottles.

He started in his kitchen. Every evening, he made coffee, let it get cold and put it into bottles. He designed a simple label with a picture of a sun and the words "Carlos Cold Coffee." Then he put a label on every bottle by hand.

On Saturdays, he sold his bottles at a market in the park. At first, he sold only 20 bottles a day. But consumers liked the taste, and they came back every week. Many consumers today want less waste, so Carlos had another idea. If people brought back an empty bottle, they got 1 dollar off the next one. Every Sunday, he washed the old bottles in hot water so he could use them again. Washing hundreds of bottles was hard work, but he didn't mind.

After a year, Carlos had 300 existing customers. He wanted to expand the business, but he wasn't sure how. His friend Dan, who owned a small restaurant, gave him some advice. "Before you expand, you need a solid plan," Dan said. "Your existing customers are happy. Don't lose them."

So Carlos wrote a solid plan. He found a small kitchen to rent, bought a machine to wash the bottles and hired an assistant.

Then a chain of 8 food stores contacted him. The chain wanted to sell his coffee in every branch. "Consumers in our stores are looking for local products," the manager said. "Your label is simple and beautiful, and that's what they want."

First, Carlos sold his coffee in 2 branches to see what would happen. The bottles were gone in 3 days. A month later, the coffee was in all 8 branches of the chain. Carlos still goes to the market every Saturday, because he doesn't want to forget his first customers.

Questions:
What did Carlos sell?
He sold cold coffee in glass bottles.
What was on the label?
The label had a picture of a sun and the words "Carlos Cold Coffee."
What happened when people brought back an empty bottle?
They got 1 dollar off the next one.
How many existing customers did Carlos have after a year?
He had 300 existing customers.
What advice did Dan give Carlos?
He said that before Carlos expanded, he needed a solid plan.
How many branches did the chain have?
The chain had 8 branches.
Why does Carlos still go to the market?
He doesn't want to forget his first customers.

lessons.title: From Attorney to Artist
lessons.summary: Ruth leaves her job as an attorney, opens a painting studio and teaches classes.
lessons.text:
Ruth was an attorney for 20 years. She worked long hours in a big office downtown, and she was good at her job. But in her free time, she always painted. On weekends, she painted at the kitchen table in her small apartment. Her apartment was full of paintings: on the walls, on the floor and under the bed.

When Ruth turned 50, she asked herself a question: "If I could do anything, what would I do?" The answer was easy. She would paint every day.

It took her a year to get ready. She saved money, and she found a small studio near the river. The studio had big windows and a lot of light. Ruth left her job as an attorney and moved her paintings from her apartment to the studio.

At first, Ruth painted classic subjects: flowers, fruit and the river. She studied classic paintings in books and copied them to learn. Then she started doing something new. She painted small flowers and birds onto white plates. People could hang the plates on the wall or use them at dinner.

Ruth also made her own frames from old wood. Each frame was different. "A good frame shows the beauty of a painting," she says.

Now Ruth teaches painting classes in her studio on Saturday afternoons. Her students are of all ages. Some are children, and some are older than Ruth. In the first class, she always tells them, "There is beauty everywhere. You just have to look." Then she shows them how to put paint onto paper without being afraid.

One of her students, an old man named Walter, had never painted before. After a few weeks, he painted a picture of his garden. Ruth put it in a frame, and Walter hung it in his living room. "It's like magic," he told her. "Painting isn't magic," Ruth said. "It's practice. But sometimes it feels like magic."

Ruth earns less money than she earned as an attorney, but she has never been happier.

Questions:
What was Ruth's job for 20 years?
She was an attorney.
Where did Ruth paint before she had a studio?
She painted at the kitchen table in her small apartment.
What did Ruth paint at first?
At first, she painted classic subjects: flowers, fruit and the river.
What did Ruth paint onto white plates?
She painted small flowers and birds onto white plates.
What did Ruth make from old wood?
She made her own frames.
What does Ruth tell her students in the first class?
She tells them that there is beauty everywhere.
What did Walter say about painting?
He said it was like magic.

lessons.title: A New Career in Medicine
lessons.summary: Sam leaves his bank job, goes to nursing school and becomes a nurse.
lessons.text:
Sam had worked at a bank for 12 years. He earned good money, but he wasn't happy. Every day, he sat in front of a computer and looked at numbers. He had always been interested in medicine, and he wanted a job where he could help people.

One evening, he talked to his wife, Lisa. "I want to become a nurse," he said. Lisa wasn't surprised. "You have been talking about medicine for years," she said. "Why don't you do it?"

Sam was concerned about money. Nursing school would cost a lot, and he would have to go into debt. "If I left the bank, I wouldn't earn anything for 2 years," he said. "We have never had any debt. I'm concerned about that." Lisa said, "If you were happy at work, you would be happier at home, too. We can live on less for 2 years."

So Sam decided to try. He kept working at the bank during the day and studied at night. The classes were hard. There was a lot of technical language, and he had to learn the names of hundreds of medicines. Sometimes it seemed impossible. "I'm 38 years old," he told Lisa. "Learning all this at my age is impossible." "It isn't impossible," she said. "It's just slow."

After a year, Sam left the bank and started working at a hospital as a student nurse. He spent his first weeks in the emergency room. The emergency room was loud and busy, and every patient needed something different. Later, he worked in the operating room, where the doctors did operations. His job was to get the technical equipment ready and to help the patients before and after their operations.

Finally, Sam finished nursing school. Now he works as a nurse in the emergency room. He earns less than he earned at the bank, and he still has a small debt. But he isn't concerned anymore. "I love going to work," he says. "I have never been so happy."

Questions:
Where had Sam worked for 12 years?
He had worked at a bank.
Why was Sam concerned?
He was concerned about money, because nursing school would cost a lot and he would go into debt.
What did Lisa say?
She said that if he were happy at work, he would be happier at home, too.
What did Sam have to learn in his classes?
He had to learn a lot of technical language and the names of hundreds of medicines.
Where did Sam work as a student nurse?
He worked in the emergency room and in the operating room.
How does Sam feel about his job now?
He loves going to work, and he has never been so happy.

lessons.title: A Summer at the Newspaper
lessons.summary: In her diary, Jen writes about her first week of work at a small newspaper.
lessons.text:
Jen is a college student who wants to write for a newspaper one day. This summer, she is working at the Riverton Times, a small local newspaper. These are 3 entries from her diary.

Monday
Today was my first day at the newspaper. I have been dreaming about this for years! The office is small, and everyone is busy. My boss is a woman named Kate. She is very frank. When I showed her my first draft, she said, "This draft is too long. Nobody will read it." She was right, of course. I wrote a second draft, and it was much better. I like that Kate is frank. I would rather hear the truth than nice words.

Wednesday
Kate gave me my first real story. She wants me to write about a trend in our town: more and more people are riding bikes to work. First, I had to determine if the trend was real. The numbers from the city reveal something interesting: bike riding has grown by 40 percent in 2 years. I also talked to 10 people who ride to work. Most of them said the same thing: it's cheaper and healthier. I wrote a draft and sent it to Kate. She said it was good, but she asked me to add more facts.

Friday
Today I learned an important lesson. Someone sent us a photo of a huge fish from the river. It looked amazing, but Kate suspected that it was fake. "Before you put a photo in the newspaper, you have to determine if it's real," she said. We checked, and she was right: the photo was fake. Someone had made it on a computer. I had never thought about fake photos before.

In the afternoon, my bike story went on the newspaper's website, in the category "City News." It was the most popular story in that category this week! Kate said, "Good work. I suspect you'll be writing for us for a long time." I'll write a new entry next week.

Questions:
Where is Jen working this summer?
She is working at the Riverton Times, a small local newspaper.
What did Kate say about Jen's first draft?
She said the draft was too long and nobody would read it.
What trend did Jen write about?
She wrote about a trend in her town: more people are riding bikes to work.
What do the numbers from the city reveal?
They reveal that bike riding has grown by 40 percent in 2 years.
What did Kate suspect about the photo of the fish?
She suspected that the photo was fake.
In which category did the bike story go?
It went in the category "City News."

lessons.title: My Summer Job at the Pool
lessons.summary: A teenager tells about his first summer job as a lifeguard and the day he helped a boy in the water.
lessons.text:
Last summer, when I was 17, I got my first job. I worked as a lifeguard at the city pool. Before I could start, I had to take a training course for 2 weeks. We learned how to help people in the water and what to do in an emergency.

There were 6 of us at the pool, and we worked as a team. Our boss, Linda, called us "the crew." "A good crew works together," she told us on the first day. Every morning at 8, the whole crew met next to the pool before it opened.

Most of the job was watching people. We had to monitor the water all the time. Linda also taught us to monitor people's behavior. "People who are in trouble tend to be quiet," she said. "They don't shout. They tend to move their arms up and down."

The children's part of the pool was always busy. Some kids were strong in the water, but others were weak. We watched the weak ones more carefully. We also watched their behavior.

In July, the city sent our crew to work at the beach on the bay for a week. Working at the bay was different from working at the pool. The water was cold, and there were waves. We told weak swimmers to stay close to the beach.

One afternoon, the sky over the bay turned dark. A storm was coming. Linda told us to get everyone out of the water. Most people left quickly, but then I noticed a boy far from the beach. He was very quiet, and his arms were moving up and down, just like Linda had described. I ran into the water and brought him back to the beach before the storm arrived. He was scared, but he was alive and fine.

His mother thanked me again and again. "He is alive because of you," she said. I told her that it was because of Linda's training. I will never forget that afternoon on the bay.

Questions:
Where did the writer work last summer?
He worked as a lifeguard at the city pool.
What did Linda teach the crew to monitor?
She taught them to monitor the water and people's behavior.
How do people in trouble tend to behave?
They tend to be quiet and move their arms up and down.
Which children did the crew watch more carefully?
They watched the weak ones more carefully.
What happened one afternoon on the bay?
A storm was coming, and the writer brought a quiet boy back to the beach.
What did the boy's mother say?
She said that her son was alive because of the writer.

lessons.title: The Science Fair
lessons.summary: After losing last year, Lily and Omar win the state science fair with a project about plants and water.
lessons.text:
Last year, Lily and her friend Omar entered the state science fair, but they lost. Their project was about the planet Mars, and the judges said it wasn't original. The defeat was hard for them. "We have to learn from this defeat," Lily said. They decided to try again the next year.

Lily wanted to study plants in college one day, so she suggested a project about water. Many farms near their town used chemicals on their fields, and the rain carried the chemicals into the river. "Are these chemicals a threat to plants?" Lily asked.

They set up 2 glass tanks with water and small plants. In the first tank, they used clean water. In the second tank, they added a little of a common farm chemical. Every day for 6 weeks, they measured the plants and looked at their roots. The plants in the first tank grew strong, white roots. The roots in the second tank were short and brown.

Omar took photos of the roots every day, and Lily wrote down the numbers. The core question of their project was simple: does this chemical hurt plants? After 6 weeks, the answer was clear. Yes, the chemical was a threat.

Their teacher, Mr. Brooks, helped them, but he let them make their own decisions. "This is your project," he said. "Leadership means making decisions." Lily showed good leadership. After one bad week, Omar wanted to give up. "We can't give up now," Lily said. "We're almost finished."

At the state science fair, they showed the tanks, the photos and the numbers. A judge asked, "Why is this important?" Omar answered, "Clean water is at the core of life on our planet. If we protected our rivers better, we would also protect our food."

At the end of the day, the judges announced the winners. Lily and Omar had won first place! After last year's defeat, the victory felt even better. "This victory belongs to both of us," Lily told Omar. Mr. Brooks was proud of them, too. "It's a victory for good leadership," he said.

Questions:
What happened at the science fair last year?
Lily and Omar lost. It was a defeat.
What was the core question of their project?
The core question was: does this chemical hurt plants?
What did they put in the second tank?
They added a little of a common farm chemical to the water.
What did the roots in the second tank look like?
They were short and brown.
What did Mr. Brooks say about leadership?
He said that leadership means making decisions.
How did the victory feel?
After last year's defeat, the victory felt even better.

lessons.title: Choosing a College
lessons.summary: Maya tells how she chose a small liberal arts college and what she wrote in her application.
lessons.text:
My name is Maya, and last year I applied to college. I had been thinking about it since I was 15, but I still didn't know where I wanted to go. My parents wanted me to go to the big state university in our city. I wasn't sure.

One day, my teacher, Mr. Hall, told me about a small liberal arts college in a green valley 3 hours from our home. At a liberal arts college, students study many subjects, like history, art, science and philosophy, before they choose one. That sounded perfect to me, because I was interested in everything.

My parents and I visited the college in October. The valley was beautiful, with a river and old trees. We sat in a philosophy class. The teacher asked big questions, like "What makes a good life?", and the students really talked to each other. I loved it. The teaching there was very different from my high school. The classes were small, and the teachers knew every student's name.

The college also had a lot of cultural events: concerts, films and talks by writers. For me, the cultural life was an important aspect of the college. Another aspect that I liked was the work with teachers. Apart from their classes, students could work with teachers on their own projects.

For the application, I had to write a short text about my youth. I had to reflect on something that had changed me. I reflected for a long time, and I chose my grandmother. In my youth, I spent every summer with her on her farm. She taught me to work hard and to ask questions. I wrote about her, and I tried to show what made my story unique.

In April, I got a letter from the college. They had accepted me! The letter said, "Your story is unique, and we enjoyed reading it." Now my parents and I live 3 hours apart, but we talk every week. If I could choose again, I would choose the same college.

Questions:
What kind of college did Mr. Hall tell Maya about?
He told her about a small liberal arts college in a green valley.
What do students study at a liberal arts college?
They study many subjects, like history, art, science and philosophy, before they choose one.
What was different about the teaching?
The classes were small, and the teachers knew every student's name.
What did Maya have to write about for her application?
She had to write about her youth and reflect on something that had changed her.
Who did Maya write about?
She wrote about her grandmother.
What did the letter from the college say?
It said that her story was unique.

lessons.title: The Manuscript
lessons.summary: Elena, who works in a city office, writes a book in the evenings and gets an email from a book company.
lessons.text:
Elena had worked in the public sector for 15 years. She had a job in the city office, where she helped people with their forms. The work was safe, but it wasn't very interesting. For years, Elena had been writing stories in the evenings. Her dream was to write a book.

Two years ago, she started writing a book about her grandmother, who had come to America from Mexico with nothing. Every evening after work, Elena sat at her desk and turned off her phone. She called this time her "writing mode." When she was in writing mode, nobody could talk to her, not even her husband.

On the web, she found a group of writers who wanted to help each other. Every week, the members shared their work on the group's web page and gave each other advice.

After 18 months, the manuscript was finished. It was 300 pages long. Elena sent the manuscript to 5 small book companies. She waited for weeks. Then an email arrived:

"Dear Ms. Ruiz,
Thank you for sending us your manuscript. With regard to your book, we have good news. Our team loved it. It is possibly the best manuscript we have received this year, and we would like to make it into a book next spring. First, we will need the final version of the manuscript by March 1. Please note that the contract has a penalty for late work: if the final manuscript arrives late, we will pay you 10 percent less.
Best regards,
Paul Stone"

Elena read the email 3 times. Then she called her husband. "They want to make my manuscript into a real book!" she said.

She didn't leave the public sector right away. She kept her job and worked on the final manuscript in the evenings and on weekends. She finished it 2 weeks early, so there was no penalty. The book came out the next year. Now Elena is writing her second book. One day, she will possibly leave the public sector and write full time.

Questions:
Where had Elena worked for 15 years?
She had worked in the public sector, in the city office.
What was Elena's book about?
It was about her grandmother.
What did Elena find on the web?
She found a group of writers who wanted to help each other.
What did the email say about the manuscript?
It said that it was possibly the best manuscript they had received that year.
What was the penalty for late work?
If the final manuscript arrived late, they would pay her 10 percent less.
Did Elena have to pay a penalty?
No. She finished 2 weeks early, so there was no penalty.
